findings.description: BYTES_PER_TICK arithmetic is off by one byte per tick, contradicting the test's own comment.
findings.failure_scenario: estimatedFramedBytes(record) = 1 (flags) + 5 + id.length + (version?10:0) + 5 + payload.length. With id="d" (1 byte) and no version, the constant overhead is 1+5+1+0+5 = 12, not 11. PAYLOAD is sized as BYTES_PER_TICK - 11 (131061 bytes), so each append actually contributes 131073 bytes, not the claimed exactly-131072 (verified by direct computation, reproduced with a standalone Java snippet). The comment '1 MiB/8 = 131072 divides EXACTLY -- no rounding drift accumulating' is therefore not accurate: there is 1 byte/tick of drift, ~960 bytes over the full 2-minute lengthen delay. This does not change the test's pass/fail outcome (the drift is 0.00076% of the modeled rate, negligible next to the 40%/90% fillRatio thresholds and the +/-20% rate tolerance) and both mutations I ran (the documented direction-swap and my own tested boundary flip) behaved identically with or without this off-by-one. Purely a factual inaccuracy in an inline comment, not a test-weakening defect.

findings.description: A `>=`-to-`>` boundary flip on the intervalLengthenDelay comparison in Accumulator.adaptInterval survives this test undetected.
findings.failure_scenario: Mutated `nowMillis - lowStreakStartMillis >= config.intervalLengthenDelay().toMillis()` to `>` and reran IntervalPutRateTest: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, test still passes. At the floor's 250ms cadence this mutation only delays settling by one flush cycle (~250ms), well inside the test's own 1-second settle-timing tolerance, so it is invisible here. This is NOT a suite-level gap, though: AccumulatorTest already exercises this exact boundary at the unit level (`theIntervalDoesNotLengthenBeforeTheSustainedDelayElapses` at 'one millisecond short' and `theIntervalLengthensToTheCeilingOnceFillRatioSustainsLowForTheFullDelay` at 'exactly the sustained delay', both from the already-shipped M3.3). Recording this because the task asked for any surviving mutation to be named, not because it represents missing coverage -- boundary precision correctly belongs to the T0 unit tier, not this T1 sustained-traffic integration test.

notes: Verified independently by running the actual test and the actual mutation (not just reading the diff): (1) IntervalPutRateTest is genuinely green against the unmodified Accumulator.java (./gradlew :ingest:test --tests ... --rerun-tasks -> BUILD SUCCESSFUL). (2) Applied the exact claimed mutation (swap ceiling/floor targets between the high- and low-fillRatio branches of Accumulator.adaptInterval) and reran: genuine, clean red -- 'java.lang.AssertionError: interval never settled at the ceiling within PT4M' at IntervalPutRateTest.java:132, executed in ~1s wall-clock (TestClock only, no sleep), no hang, no OOM. Reverted, confirmed byte-identical to the original (empty git diff) and green again. (3) Confirmed the give-up bound (4 simulated minutes) is comfortably tight for the correct path (~2min lengthenDelay + 60s window + a flush-alignment margin, i.e. ~180s against a 240s bound) while being fast/clean on the wrong path, matching the stated rationale about MemoryBinStore retaining every PUT under the 512m test heap. (4) No Thread.sleep/System.currentTimeMillis anywhere in the test -- only TestClock.advance. (5) The three assertions (settle-timing, stays-at-ceiling, measured-rate) are not redundant: a bug that shortens back to the floor mid-window would blow the rate assertion (many more PUTs than the +/-20% band allows) even without the stays-at-ceiling check firing first, and a bug that settles too early or too late is caught by the settle-timing assertion specifically, which a rate-only check would not distinguish from 'eventually got there'. (6) Confirmed the modeled traffic and the production SegmentPublisher/CountingBinStore/IngestConfig.defaults values referenced by the test (8 MiB maxSegmentBytes, 5s ceiling, 0.4/0.9 thresholds, 2min/0 delays) match what is actually in the shipped M3.1-M3.3 code -- nothing in the test asserts against a value the production code does not itself use. Overall: this test would fail if the adaptive-interval logic under test were wrong, on the specific mutation class the task names, and the two minor findings above are documentation/tiering notes rather than blocking gaps.
